4:15pm – Take a break, shower, have dinner and clean up the kitchen.
5pm – Head home. The reason I want you to embrace your commute and work from home routine like a boss is that it sets boundaries and boundaries are a great way to maintain work and life balance.
But more importantly, a routine shows up to work on time.

A lot of people in the space are making these new DApps but they are really just using the old internet structure to communicate with each other with a centralized company controlling everything.

That’s 20 years before we’re even starting to be able to answer this question for ourselves.
By the time we get a job, we’re usually working 40 hours a week, doing something we’re not good at, not particularly happy about, and not going to be around for any significant amount of time.
By the time we retire, we’re probably not going to have answered the question yet.

We’ve spent our entire lives learning how to live for others.
Now we’re suddenly being told we have to do it for ourselves.
The most significant thing most parents and mentors can do for young people, in my opinion, is give them the tools to ask the right questions, and to think for themselves.

Now they have to figure it all out by themselves.

blocks.text: you are. A lot of people seem to make the same mistake.
They take their actions as evidence that they are capable of something.
This is not always the case. The actions you take are irrelevant.
What’s more important is how you react when the opportunity arises.
This is especially true for those who work in creative industries.
You might have a passion for photography but it doesn’t mean you can make a living out of it.
There are a lot of talented people out there.
Many of them lack creative discipline and are stuck in reactive mode.
They take the actions but don’t take a step back and review the whole process.
Is there anything you can do to improve?
I am a bit obsessed with creativity.
I’m constantly trying to improve the process.
I’m not suggesting that you should become an obsessive compulsive about the creative process.
That’s a huge burden to put yourself under.
But a slight change in perspective can go a long way.
One of the things that I’ve learnt and been doing over the last few years is that what you do has to make sense.
You can’t do random activities.
Every time you take an action, you should take some time to step back and see the bigger picture.
This helps you to identify which actions are more likely to take you in the right direction.
They are the ones that you should continue doing and work on.
It’s not about saying no to everything.
You shouldn’t discount any idea just because you don’t think it works.
It’s about taking your idea and seeing if it holds water.
Does it make sense? Or is there a better alternative?
What are the next steps? What would happen if you tried something completely different?
The best ideas are never the one that pops into our head randomly.

blocks.text: a blog, I had a “toddler moment.” My son was two years old, but he was very busy and playful, and he would play with anything that he thought was a puzzle, and sometimes, when he didn’t do well at something, he would throw a fit.
(Of course, the real challenge was to get him to stop throwing his fit—after he realized that he might lose a toy, or whatever, if he didn’t settle down.)

It occurred to me that this is exactly how many of us think about philosophy—that is, we think it’s about “getting things right,” and if we get them right, we think our philosophy has value and meaning.
But, in the past few years, I’ve begun to see things a bit differently.

I’ve begun to think that what philosophy is, is more about the “getting it done” than it is about “getting it right.” It’s less about being absolutely sure we’ve gotten the right answer, and more about just being able to say something intelligent or interesting in a way that is helpful and meaningful.
I should say that what I’m talking about is what is called pragmatism, and I would be happy to talk about that in some detail.
But, in order to do that, I’m going to make some very general, generalistic claims about philosophy that I think most of you will agree are true.
The first claim is that when people do philosophy, they do it in the service of some practical goal.
You can’t study philosophy unless you have a reason to study it.
If you don’t have a practical goal that will make you want to learn some new idea or theory or explanation, then why would you bother studying philosophy?
So, philosophy is a study that is done to achieve some practical goal.

blocks.text: schedule that required writing three hours per day.
I had no distractions. No TV. No time for lunch.
No games. No Netflix. This was my 2019 New Year’s resolution.
(As an aside, let’s hope it lasts as long as 2018’s new year’s resolutions!)
I was writing in a very structured way.
I followed an outline with chapter headings, I researched topics from the text, and I went back and re-read the entire book on a daily basis.
If it was all going well, and that’s what I was starting out with, this would take a minimum of seven months.
But I had a deadline of just two months, with no opportunity to stop.
I wasn’t sure I could pull it off in the time, but I was convinced I could at least complete one chapter a day for two weeks.
And that’s what happened. I had so much work to do in just two weeks; I didn’t want to stop, so I kept plowing ahead.
I did, and I got it done. Here’s how you can do the same.
The first step in this writing process is to make sure you know what you’re going to write.
You have to start somewhere. Writing a novel is a complicated business.
How would you write one without an outline?
That seems impossible. But it’s not.
And you can do it. This one step is crucial in getting started.
And that’s why I recommend making an outline in the middle of June.
Because when the conference is happening, you don’t want to think about what you’re going to write.
When you know what you’re going to write, writing it is easy.
It is a walk in the park. But don’t just create an outline and think it’s over.
When you have it in your hands, look over it.

blocks.text: , given the uncertainty and fear that surrounds us.
This is partly due to the way in which I think about refuge.
To the Buddhist, a refuge is more than just a place to go when you’re scared.
It’s a place to stand and to serve.
The first refuge is Buddhism, the second dharma, and the third sangha.
But the fourth one? The fourth is myself.
It’s always with me, and that’s where true refuge is found.
This notion is important because it’s something I often fail to grasp, especially in times like these.
Instead, I find refuge in what the government and media tell us about the pandemic, whether that means my job or the health of my loved ones.
In this moment, the media and the government are preaching a message of fear and self-preservation.
It’s a message I’m learning to ignore, which may be why the three refuges have become so relevant.
If we don’t keep ourselves grounded, we’re in danger of succumbing to what I’ve called the “virus of the day.” The other day, we worried about getting sick.
Now, because of a government shutdown, we’re worried about getting fired and losing our homes, which may lead to an increase in suicide rates.
Fear and anxiety are very common.
In a crisis like this, it’s understandable to feel panicked, but the problem is in allowing fear to define you.
When I think of fear, I think of a beast of burden.
Fear is something that people feel, and it can feel very real.
But if you give it power, you let it control you.
It makes you believe in the worst, and it makes you want to do anything to get out of it.
